title: Fatality report says Edmonton police officers lack first-aid training
article: Edmonton police Const. Dan Furman was bleeding to death in 2006 from three gunshot wounds, but most of his fellow officers were in shock and unable to help because they lacked training.

The same officers also didn't help the man they shot nine times, even though the police force's own policy required them to render first aid until paramedics arrived, says a fatality inquiry report released Monday.
"This emphasizes the limitations that the basic first-aid course affords to Edmonton Police Service members when confronted with medical emergencies," says the report.
Darren Cardinal was hiding in the basement of a duplex armed with a gun and possibly high on drugs when he was confronted by police in June 2006.
Furman attempted to shot him with a Taser but missed and Cardinal shot the officer three times at close range. Two officers in an adjoining room then shot the gunman nine or 10 times as he fled.

Cardinal, 26, was still awake and talking when paramedics arrived. Police had handcuffed him, but Cardinal appeared to be in shock and police were not providing him with any treatment or assistance, says the report.
The report credits Const. Jason Mitchell with saving Furman's life, saying he used pressure to control heavy bleeding from an artery pierced by one of the bullets.

"It was obvious from the evidence that the (police) on the scene were in shock and, except for Mitchell, did not have the training to provide any meaningful medical attention to either Furman or Cardinal," the report concludes.
Mitchell had received advanced first-aid training to deal with gunshot victims in the military before he joined the police force.

After spending eight months recovering from his wounds, Furman worked with medical experts to develop a first-aid training course to upgrade Edmonton police to a level of training closer to what Mitchell received.
But the fatality report says Furman's proposal "was put on hold because of budgetary concerns."
This does not sit well with Alberta Solicitor General Fred Lindsay.

"I believe our officers should be trained to offer assistance to people who are injured when they carry out their duties," said Lindsay. "So I will be reviewing the police training standards in this province to view exactly that."
"To not feel competent enough to be able to do anything to help a fellow officer when he's injured is somewhat shocking to me," he said.
However, Lindsay said he's not prepared to provide any additional money to Edmonton police to upgrade first-aid training for the force's 1,700 officers.
Edmonton police spokesman Jeff Wuite said the force was hoping to begin a pilot program within a few weeks based on Furman's recommendation.
"Nothing has been approved yet," Wuite said in an interview. "We're hoping to roll it out for our members next month."
Wuite explained that all front-line officers are already trained in first aid and CPR and they have to re-qualify every two years.
"But this recommendation goes behind initial first care and is something that would be very specific to officer down situations," he said.
